newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac says hopes for early solution on EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says hopes for early solution on EMU pact.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Wednesday he believed European Union leaders could resolve a dispute over an EU budget pact at a summit next week, but stressed the need for a more socially acceptable Europe.

Earlier in the day, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said the new left-wing government wanted an early solution to differences over the pact but insisted it must win its demand for a greater focus on growth and jobs before signing any deal.

"I want it and hope for it and, to tell the truth, I believe so," Chirac told reporters when asked if the pact -- on deficit control after the launch of the euro single currency -- could be signed at the EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

"Europe is not only a financial or monetary issue, even if these issues are capital. Europe is also men and women who must be taken into account," Chirac said after talks at the Elysee presidential palace with British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Analysts say Paris is signalling a willingness in principle to approve the pact at the EU summit provided France can drive a hard bargain in making unemployment the top priority in Europe.

"We are clearly going to find a solution. If we can move forward quickly, it is obviously better. No one wants to drag things out for the sake of it," Strauss-Kahn said after a cabinet meeting on Wednesday. "The question is to know how we can obtain the balance we are seeking."

France's new Socialist-led government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary victory on June 1, is seeking better balance in Europe between budget discipline and price control on the one hand and growth and jobs on the other.

At a finance ministers' meeting in Luxembourg on Monday it withheld approval of the EU "stability pact" limiting the budget deficits of states which join a single currency, stunning EU partners who then rushed to say they too had always stressed jobs as a priority.

Strauss-Kahn has said France is simply trying to enforce the 1991 Maastricht Treaty which calls for greater economic policy coordination among European countries and stresses growth and jobs alongside fiscal discipline and price control.
"Let's apply the treaty and not just 10 percent of the treaty," a source close to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said.
"The French government merely wants to respect the spirit and letter of the treaty," former European Commission president Jacques Delors, an adviser to Jospin, said this week.

The government is trying to restore a balance reached between Paris and Bonn when the treaty was negotiated in the early 1990s, which it fears has been lost in a German-dominated approach in recent years.

Germany has always emphasised the need for an independent central bank, guaranteeing price and currency stability. France has pushed for a more political vision stressing the need for economic growth to boost employment.
In arguing its case, the government is also trying to fulfil campaign pledges to turn Europe away from austerity and win support for France's call for a European "economic government".
Faced with a very tight EU timetable -- with the Amsterdam summit deadline fixed before it came to power -- France is trying to turn the shortage of time to its advantage.
"We are trying to capitalise on this momentum to get a number of things through, given that all our partners know they have to negotiate," a government source said.

"I'm sure the government would like to reach an agreement this weekend," UBS economist Darren Williams said. "But obviously they are not going to sacrifice all their election pledges just to come up with an agreement on time."
Jospin has declined comment on whether he would sign up to the stability pact at the Amsterdam summit, which he will attend alongside President Jacques Chirac.

But Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said after talks in Paris on Tuesday that Jospin had told him the signature did not need to wait until he made his policy speech to parliament on June 19. That lifted one major potential obstacle to a deal in Amsterdam.
What remains is the language of a declaration -- which could either be added to the stability pact or made as a separate "growth pact" stressing the need for growth and jobs.
Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, has been given the job of trying to work out the wording with his EU colleagues.
Blair told reporters he and Chirac agreed that Europe needed to focus more on social as well as economic issues.
"We both agreed that European construction must concentrate on key economic and social priorities...such as producing greater employment and social inclusion," he said.
Sources at the French president's office said Chirac had "made a strong plea to the British prime minister to help the French government achieve its aims".
